items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1975-02-03
items.q: I did have the opportunity to see and meet Bolden

ctx.x: And did you go to hear music with him?

Uh, no, but he was the one who brought, who bought most of the records that came into the house. Mm-hm. And, uh, uh, of course we had all the early jazz records, largely because of the fact that he knew the musicians himself, and, uh, and I came to know many of the musicians when I was very young. I remember, for example, some social function that went on in the house when I was very young, for which Papa Celestan's band was hired. And, uh, while I don't remember who the individual musicians were, my first…
Well, was your uncle hiring bands?

items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1976-02-19
items.q: when you get someone like Buddy Bowden for instance who was so inspired to play jazz

ctx.x: the jazz form oh no not at all nothing those particular things have nothing in common at all the blues is a set eight or twelve bar form of mainly vocal music which is is extremely rigid and traditionally performed by one or two people mostly as a vocal music now there is none of that element that occurs in the jazz at all the the gospel music too is a another indigenous black form but you didn't have an influx of black gospel musicians to Chicago under the guise of jazz because as a matter of fact I tell you…

now okay granted blues and jazz and gospel and rag well I don't know about ragtime we're talking about something else okay okay we won't are separate forms of music they have their own forms but when you get someone like Buddy Bowden for instance who was so inspired to play jazz by by going to the local Baptist church and listening to the I don't believe that to the call and response pattern and yeah I just don't believe that you don't believe that that the jazz musicians were influenced very much by the call and…

believe that the that the that the call and response pattern is characteristic of both kinds of music and I believe that they derive from a common source of both gospel music and jazz music and I believe that they derive from the common source of the African West African tribal music yeah and this pattern that you discuss does fundamentally represent that part of the jazz which does represent the blacks contribution to it all right for the most part okay that's true but I think it's a fairly large contribution…

Uh, I don't even know if he was that much interested in it. Uh-huh. You know, we just heard some musicians around town like we all did. Yeah. And I assumed that he responded positively to it, but I'm, I'm not, uh, the really great musicians were contemporaries of his, so I doubt whether he'd have been influenced by anybody. Uh-huh. Uh, I'm sure he heard Bolden, but I don't think that he had a clear picture in his mind of who he was. You really, you do think even at his age he would have heard Bolden?
